::: {#case .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-case">
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">1 · The puzzle</p><p>The theoretical curve of a turbine type covers every wind speed but not how a turbine actually operates. Measured records show real behaviour, including scatter, stops and <span class="lx-term" data-term="curtailment">curtailment</span>, but they are noisy.</p><p class="lx-hint">Words first: a <span class="lx-term" data-term="power-curve">power curve</span> gives a turbine's output at each wind speed. Measured points scatter, so a fit allows many plausible curves, a band; a theoretical curve is extra information covering every speed.</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">2 · The question in one sentence</p><p class="lx-case-q">Can <span class="lx-term" data-term="multi-fidelity">multi-fidelity</span> <span class="lx-term" data-term="gaussian-process">Gaussian process</span> regression, combining a theoretical power curve with limited measured data, improve probabilistic wind turbine power-curve estimation?</p><p class="lx-hint">Question type: predictive (what power, with what uncertainty?), with an evaluative part (better than records alone?).</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">3 · Scale and boundary</p><ul><li><b>Inside:</b> one wind farm's measured operating records (<span class="lx-term" data-term="scada">SCADA</span>) from the open <span class="lx-term" data-term="sdwpf">SDWPF</span> dataset, and the theoretical power curve of the turbine type; point scores for nine test turbines, probabilistic scores for one.</li><li><b>Left out:</b> other wind farms, other datasets and other theoretical curves.</li></ul></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">4 · Decisions, goal and rules, in words</p><ul><li><b>Decisions:</b> which few hundred measured points to train on, drawn from a <span class="lx-term" data-term="kernel-density-estimate">kernel density estimate</span> of the records, and how to link the theoretical curve to them: a linear or a nonlinear multi-fidelity model.</li><li><b>Goal:</b> a power curve given as a probability distribution, not a single line.</li><li><b>Rules:</b> every model is scored on the same turbines, with point metrics (such as <span class="lx-term" data-term="rmse">RMSE</span>) and probabilistic metrics (<span class="lx-term" data-term="pinball-loss">pinball loss</span>, <span class="lx-term" data-term="sharpness">sharpness</span>, <span class="lx-term" data-term="calibration">reliability</span>).</li></ul><p class="lx-hint">Scores: RMSE, the typical size of a miss; pinball loss, a charge for misses and for width; sharpness, how narrow a band is; reliability, whether a 90% band holds about 90% of new measurements.</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">5 · Data and method</p><ul><li>Linear (<span class="lx-term" data-term="autoregressive-fusion">autoregressive</span>) and nonlinear multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression fuse the turbine type's theoretical power curve (low fidelity) with a few hundred kernel-density-sampled SCADA points from the open SDWPF dataset (high fidelity), and are compared with single-fidelity regression on point and probabilistic metrics.</li><li>The kernel density sample keeps the shape of the scatter without manual cleaning; a compact training set matters because a Gaussian process solve grows with the cube of the training points.</li></ul></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">6 · What came out, and where it holds</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:uq-mfgpr"><p>In the reported nine-turbine test, nonlinear multi-fidelity regression achieved lower RMSE for most turbines; performance depended on the evaluation metric.</p><p>The probabilistic multi-fidelity model was also able to generate confidence intervals that encompassed the measured power.</p><footer>From: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1115/detc2023-114762">Li et al., ASME IDETC 2023</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint">Holds when: one wind farm in one open dataset, one generic theoretical curve, and about two hundred sampled measurements; probabilistic scores for one turbine. Leaves out: other wind farms and datasets.</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Related project · uncertainty at plants without measurements</p>
<details class="lx-deeper cf8-related"><summary><span class="k">Optional</span>Read its question and method</summary><div class="lx-deeper-body">
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:wind-uq"><p>In a research project (2022–2023), the course author worked on this question: can uncertainty metrics of a wind power model's inputs (weather data products, forecast ensembles and turbine-level data) predict calibrated plant-level power uncertainty at wind plants that have no power measurements?</p><p>The course author developed the surrogate-modeling workflow: calibrated uncertainty targets, surrogate models and validation on held-out plants.</p><p>Inputs: uncertainty metrics of four kinds: how a series varies over time (moving windows), how data sources disagree, how widely a forecast ensemble spreads, and how values vary across a plant's turbines (a <span class="lx-term" data-term="variogram">variogram</span>).</p><p>Targets: at plants with power measurements, the scale of a predictive distribution around the point forecast, chosen to minimize pinball loss.</p><p><span class="lx-term" data-term="surrogate-model">Surrogates</span>: Gaussian process regression and other regressors learn a mapping from the metrics to that scale, then predict probabilistic power at plants without measurements.</p><p>Validation holds out whole plants, scored with pinball loss, <span class="lx-term" data-term="crps">CRPS</span> and reliability, with recalibration of the predictive distributions.</p><p>The project has no paper. The public framework is a fresh implementation tested on synthetic data; project data and results are not public.</p><footer>This work was developed based upon funding from the Alliance for Sustainable Energy, LLC, Managing and Operating Contractor for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory for the U.S. Department of Energy.</footer></blockquote>
</div></details>
<p class="lx-hint">Question and method only: no results.</p></div>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive" data-learn="cf8" data-src="../assets/learn/data/cf8-power-curves-from-scarce-data.json">
```

## The idea behind it, then where the result holds
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-interactive" data-learn="cf8-idea" data-src="../assets/learn/data/cf8-power-curves-from-scarce-data.json ../assets/learn/data/m09-surrogates-uq.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- cf8-idea:start (written from the toy model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">From a band on the curve to a band on the capacity factor (illustrative)</p><p>Lesson M9's toy turbine and records: invented round numbers, not the study's data. The maker's curve gives a capacity factor of 32.4%; the field curve, hidden from the fits, 31.3%.</p><p class="lx-hint">The band is the fitted curve's uncertainty only: the expected capacity factor, with the wind-speed mix and the fit's settings held fixed. It leaves out year-to-year weather and operating changes.</p><p class="lx-hint">90% band: if the fitted model is right, the expected capacity factor lies inside it with probability 0.9.</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table cf8-res"><caption class="lx-hint">Expected capacity factor with its 90% band from the fitted curve, in percentage points</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Records</th><th scope="col">Measured records only</th><th scope="col">Records + maker's curve</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>16</td><td class="n">31.3% ± 2.8</td><td class="n">31.0% ± 1.5</td></tr><tr><td>24</td><td class="n">31.1% ± 1.4</td><td class="n">31.3% ± 1.2</td></tr><tr><td>32</td><td class="n">31.0% ± 1.3</td><td class="n">31.1% ± 1.0</td></tr><tr><td>48</td><td class="n">31.1% ± 0.9</td><td class="n">31.2% ± 0.9</td></tr><tr><td>64</td><td class="n">31.0% ± 0.8</td><td class="n">31.2% ± 0.8</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-eyebrow">How the capacity factor is averaged (the maker's curve)</p><p class="lx-hint">Capacity factor = the sum, over wind speeds, of share of the year's hours × power, divided by the 2,000 kW rating. Every curve on this page is averaged the same way.</p><p class="lx-hint">The wind-speed mix, the share of the year's hours at each speed, is an illustrative <span class="lx-term" data-term="weibull">Weibull distribution</span>: shape k = 2 (no unit), scale c = 8 m/s, the same for every curve.</p><p class="lx-hint">Output below 3 m/s and above 20 m/s (0.2% of hours) counts as zero.</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table cf8-bins"><caption class="lx-hint">Rounded; the total is summed in 0.1 m/s steps before rounding</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Wind speed</th><th scope="col">Share of the year's hours</th><th scope="col">Maker's curve, mean power</th><th scope="col">Adds to the capacity factor, points</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">below 3 m/s</th><td class="n">13.1%</td><td class="n">0 kW</td><td class="n">0.0</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">3–5 m/s</th><td class="n">19.2%</td><td class="n">58 kW</td><td class="n">0.6</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">5–7 m/s</th><td class="n">21.2%</td><td class="n">260 kW</td><td class="n">2.8</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">7–9 m/s</th><td class="n">18.3%</td><td class="n">649 kW</td><td class="n">5.9</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">9–11 m/s</th><td class="n">13.1%</td><td class="n">1,288 kW</td><td class="n">8.4</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">11–13 m/s</th><td class="n">8.0%</td><td class="n">1,960 kW</td><td class="n">7.8</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">13–15 m/s</th><td class="n">4.2%</td><td class="n">2,000 kW</td><td class="n">4.2</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">15–20 m/s</th><td class="n">2.8%</td><td class="n">2,000 kW</td><td class="n">2.8</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">above 20 m/s</th><td class="n">0.2%</td><td class="n">counted as 0</td><td class="n">0.0</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">All hours</th><td class="n">100%</td><td></td><td class="n">32.4</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<!-- cf8-idea:end -->
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>Add measured points one by one</h3></header>
<div class="explainer" data-explainer="uq-mfgpr">
<ol class="ex-fallback lx-ex-static"><li>A Gaussian process fitted to a few measured points is uncertain wherever the points are sparse, so its band widens between them.</li><li>A multi-fidelity model also learns from the turbine's theoretical power curve, which covers every wind speed, and uses it to fill in the shape between measurements, so the band can narrow there.</li><li>In the paper's test, the result depended on the evaluation metric.</li></ol>
</div>
<p class="lx-hint">A separate example with synthetic numbers, from the course author's open explainer: not the study's data or results.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Its bands, like the toy's, describe uncertainty about the average curve. A band for one new measurement must also hold measurement and operating scatter, so it is wider.</p>
<!-- cf8-extext:start (written from the explainer's own model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Text version of the explainer: its synthetic turbine at the slider's start, 5 measured points</summary><div class="cf8-ex-table"><p class="lx-hint">From the explainer's own synthetic data: estimates and 95% bands of the curve at each region's center, in kW.</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table cf8-ex"><caption class="lx-hint">With 5 measured points</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Wind speed</th><th scope="col">Points there</th><th scope="col">True curve (hidden)</th><th scope="col">Data only, 95% band</th><th scope="col">Curve + data, 95% band</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>0–5 m/s</td><td>1</td><td>8 kW</td><td>93 kW ± 236</td><td>71 kW ± 136</td></tr><tr><td>5–10 m/s</td><td>2</td><td>360 kW</td><td>481 kW ± 142</td><td>417 kW ± 128</td></tr><tr><td>10–15 m/s</td><td>2</td><td>1,745 kW</td><td>1,794 kW ± 112</td><td>1,741 kW ± 93</td></tr><tr><td>15–20 m/s</td><td>0</td><td>1,877 kW</td><td>1,243 kW ± 781</td><td>1,811 kW ± 227</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-hint">These statistical bands do not know that power has limits: they can reach below zero or above the rating, as at 0–5 m/s.</p></div></details>
<!-- cf8-extext:end -->
</div>
```

## Check yourself, then try it
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="cf8-myth">
<!-- cf8-myth:start (written from the toy model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="exact" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A power curve fitted to measurements gives the turbine's capacity factor exactly.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In the toy, 16 records give 31.3% ± 2.8 points (90% band of the expected value, from the fitted curve alone); even 64 records leave ± 0.8.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="maker" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The maker's power curve gives a turbine's real capacity factor.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In the toy the maker's curve gives 32.4% and the field curve 31.3%: gusts and losses take 1.2 points.</p></details>
</div>
<!-- cf8-myth:end -->
</div>
<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="cf8">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="score" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Invented numbers, not the study's: two “90%” bands are checked on 100 new measurements. Band A, 150 kW wide on average, holds 62; band B, 300 kW wide, holds 89. Which better matches its claimed 90%?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A: a narrower band always matches better</li><li data-value="b">B: it holds about the 90% it claims</li><li data-value="c">Neither: coverage cannot be checked on 100 measurements</li><li data-value="d">A: it has the lower RMSE</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>B. It holds 89 of 100, close to the 90 it claims; A holds only 62. Coverage alone does not rank them: pinball loss also charges for how far misses fall outside a band.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-case-try">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Try it yourself</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Optional, about 30 minutes each; needs Python 3.10 or later (<a href="b02-python-data.html">lesson B2</a>).</p>
<p><b>Try it yourself:</b> the framework fits the three models to an invented turbine type and wind farm in a few seconds.</p>
<p>Change the training size and the kernel-density bandwidth, or compare linear and nonlinear fusion on a test function.</p>
<p>Its numbers say nothing about any real turbine.</p>
<ul>
<li>Run <code>python examples/sensitivity.py</code>: at 50, 100, 200 and 400 training points, which model has the lowest RMSE, and does the order hold at every size?</li>
<li>Run <code>python examples/probabilistic.py</code> and compare the coverage at each nominal level with the level itself.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/mfgpr-wind-power-curve">mfgpr-wind-power-curve</a>: public example repository · MIT license · synthetic data.</p>
<p><b>Try it yourself:</b> the framework runs end to end on invented plants in about half a minute; another example compares target choices against a <span class="lx-term" data-term="negative-control">negative control</span>.</p>
<p>Its numbers say nothing about any real plant, data product or forecast system.</p>
<ul>
<li>Run <code>python examples/minimal.py</code>, then <code>python examples/validation_design.py</code>. A surrogate is useful only if it beats a constant baseline on held-out plants.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/wind-uq-surrogate">wind-uq-surrogate</a>: public example repository · MIT license · synthetic data.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">This work was developed based upon funding from the Alliance for Sustainable Energy, LLC, Managing and Operating Contractor for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory for the U.S. Department of Energy.</p>
</div>
```
